newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Enron revises Portland General acquisition.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Enron revises Portland General acquisition.

text.p: Texas gas giant Enron Corp. on Monday revised the terms of its proposed $2.1 billion acquisition of Portland General Corp. by increasing benefits for customers and lowering the payout to Portland General shareholders.

Houston-based Enron said it would guarantee a $141 million rate cut for customers of Oregon-based Portland General Electric Co. but lower the ratio to 0.9825-for-one from one-for-one at which shares would be paid to Portland shareholders.
"The deal is less attractive for Portland shareholders than the original transaction, but it's a lot better than no deal at all," Linda Byus, an analyst at Nesbitt Burns Securities Inc. said.

The revision comes in response to the decision announced Friday by staff of the Oregon Public Utility Commission to recommend that Enron's acquisition of Portland General be denied unless the companies come up with rate reductions of at least $141 million for Portland's electric utility customers.
"It looks like Enron blinked," Raymond Moore, an analyst at Dillon Read & Co. said. "The staff got what they wanted."
From the standpoint of investors, the new terms eliminate any concerns that Enron was considering backing out of the deal, he added.

Portland General's stock closed at $35.125, up $3.125, and Enron's stock closed at $37.50, up $1.625, both on the New York Stock Exchange. At that price, Portland General's shareholders would receive $36.84 a share and the deal would be worth $1.89 billion.
Ken Lay, Enron's chief executive officer, said Portland shareholders would receive about 1 million shares less than they would have under the original deal.
Portland General said the decision to accept fewer Enron shares reflected the improved chance of getting the deal past Oregon regulators.
"This is a very modest reduction in the ratio in return for increasing the likelihood that the merger will go ahead," Portland's Chief Executive Ken Harrison said.
"This merger represents not just the best course of action today, but the best course we could see in any reasonable timeframe," he added.
Mike Allegre, a spokesman for the Oregon Public Utility Commission, said staff had not yet received full details on the new proposal, but expected to meet with the companies this week.
"We can't comment until we know the exact terms and conditions," of the offer, he noted.
Lay said a timeframe for implementing the rate cut was up to the commission, which had initially indicated a four-year term for ratepayers to reap merger-related benefits.
Asked whether he expected job cuts as a result of the merger, Lay said there would not be largescale layoffs.
"This is not a merger about layoffs. We do not have overlapping businesses," Lay said.
The Oregon commission is scheduled to announce a final decision on the merger in early June, and Portland General's shareholders will vote on the new terms at the company's annual meeting on June 24.
Moore at Dillon Read described the planned merger as "an alright deal for Enron, but a great deal for Portland General."
"You want to be the acquiree, not the acquiror, because companies tend to overpay. I don't think anyone else would be paying what Enron is," he said.
